extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic account of Theranos and its regulatory, legal, and technological issues
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing the history, technology, partnerships, regulatory actions, legal proceedings, and public coverage of a single company (Theranos). Suitable for readers seeking a neutral overview and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA medical device classification and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The FDA classified Theranos's device (the nanotainer) as a Class II medical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a Class II device Theranos would need to use special labels, meet certain performance standards and perform post-market surveillance of the device. The article contrasts this with Theranos's assertion the nanotainer was Class I (not subject to these regulatory requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of blood-collection containers and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Blood-collection containers and devices must be validated under actual or simulated use conditions and reviewed/approved by designated individuals prior to issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FDA inspection reports stated Theranos's containers were 'not validated under actual or simulated use conditions' and 'were not reviewed and not approved by designated individual(s) prior to issuance', citing this as a regulatory failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with FDA Title 21 (regulatory requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory devices and processes must comply with FDA Title 21 regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FDA inspections in 2014 and 2015 resulted in multiple observed violations of FDA Title 21 Regulations for Theranos; adherence to Title 21 is presented as a baseline regulatory requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLIA certification and CMS laboratory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical laboratories must hold and maintain valid CLIA certificates and comply with CMS rules; noncompliance can lead to revocation and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS revoked Theranos's CLIA certificate and issued sanctions prohibiting the company's owners from owning/operating a certified clinical laboratory for two years, suspended approval to receive Medicare/Medicaid payments, and imposed a civil monetary penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding practices that create 'immediate jeopardy' to patient safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory practices must not create 'immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS reported Theranos's Newark lab caused 'immediate jeopardy' due to a warfarin dosing test; this standard triggers urgent enforcement actions like suspension of services and facility certification revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-reviewed publication and independent validation of test performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about novel medical testing technologies should be supported by peer-reviewed research and independent validation studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that no peer-reviewed research from Theranos had been published, that the company promised data would be published, and that independent studies (e.g., Journal of Clinical Investigation) found significant problems with Theranos test results. Independent verification (e.g., Cleveland Clinic validation) is cited as important for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, reliability, and equivalence to standard laboratory services
rubrics_metrics.description: New testing methods must demonstrate accuracy, reliability, and equivalence (low interservice variability) compared with established laboratory services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study reported Theranos results were 'flagged outside their normal range 1.6× more often than other testing services', 68% of measurements 'showed significant interservice variability', and lipid panel results were 'nonequivalent' — these metrics are used to evaluate test validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in methods and disclosure of machines/processes used
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should be transparent about whether proprietary devices or conventional machines are used to run tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wall Street Journal reported Theranos used traditional blood-testing machines instead of its Edison devices for many tests; lack of transparency about methods contributed to loss of credibility and partner withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust quality management systems and documented approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratories must have functioning quality management, documented review and approval processes, and internal controls for test methods and consumables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FDA inspectors criticized Theranos for poor quality management and missing documented approvals (e.g., containers not reviewed/approved). Effective quality systems are implied as necessary to meet regulatory expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely reporting, corrective action, and result remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: When inaccuracies or failures are discovered, companies must promptly report issues, void or correct invalid results, and take corrective operational actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theranos voided two years of results from its Edison device and announced that about 1% of test results had been voided or corrected. The company also voluntarily suspended tests (except FDA-approved HSV-1) after inspections. Such actions and clear communication are described as remediation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent external verification and partnerships for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent verification by reputable institutions (e.g., Cleveland Clinic) and credible partnerships support claims about new medical technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites partnerships (Walgreens, Safeway, Cleveland Clinic) and notes Cleveland Clinic agreed to complete a validation study; loss or termination of such partnerships followed investigative reports and regulatory findings, reducing credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scientific and technical expertise in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards and advisory panels should include relevant scientific and technical expertise to evaluate proprietary medical technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theranos's board was criticized for being composed largely of directors with diplomatic or military backgrounds; the later inclusion of medical advisory board members with clinical chemistry expertise is presented as an effort to bolster credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful disclosures to investors, partners, patients, and regulators (fraud/compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications to investors, partners, patients, and regulators must be truthful and not conceal known unreliability or inaccuracies; false or misleading statements can lead to SEC civil charges and criminal indictments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC alleged Theranos and its executives engaged in an 'elaborate, years-long fraud' deceiving investors about the capabilities of its portable analyzer; indictments alleged defendants concealed knowledge of unreliability. The article uses these proceedings to illustrate legal consequences for deceptive conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with consumer-protection and advertising laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must avoid false advertising and comply with consumer-protection statutes (e.g., Arizona Consumer Fraud Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theranos signed a consent decree over alleged violations of the Arizona Consumer Fraud Act, including false advertisement and inaccurate blood testing, and agreed to refund residents for tests — demonstrating enforcement under consumer protection law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate handling of whistleblowers and non-retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should not attempt to intimidate or legally threaten sources who raise concerns about safety or accuracy; whistleblower reports to authorities are legitimate avenues for raising compliance issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theranos sent lawyers after sources for the Wall Street Journal story and attempted to stop them from providing information, while employees (e.g., Tyler Shultz) reported concerns to regulators under alias — the article highlights whistleblowing and company attempts to suppress it as central to the exposure.
